questions.question: A decision maker chooses an action $a\in A$; each action induces a probability distribution over outcomes $x$, and $v(x)$ is the payoff of outcome $x$. Which action does expected payoff maximisation select?
options: An action maximising the expected outcome $\mathbb{E}[x\mid a]$
An action whose best possible outcome has the highest payoff
An action maximising $\mathbb{E}[v(x)\mid a]$ over $a\in A$
An action whose most likely outcome has the highest payoff

questions.question: A decision maker chooses an action $a\in A$; each action induces a probability distribution over outcomes $x$, and $v(x)$ is the payoff of outcome $x$. Two decision makers rank all outcomes in the same order but use different payoff functions. Must they choose the same action?
options: Yes: identical rankings of outcomes always give identical choices.
Yes, provided both payoff functions are strictly increasing.
No: they can disagree only when outcomes are certain.
No: payoff differences, not only the ranking, affect expected payoffs.

questions.question: A decision maker chooses an action $a\in A$; each action induces a probability distribution over outcomes $x$, and $v(x)$ is the payoff of outcome $x$. Suppose every action leads to a single outcome with probability $1$. What does expected payoff maximisation reduce to?
options: Choosing any action, since without uncertainty all are equally good
Choosing the action whose sure outcome has the highest payoff
Choosing the action with the highest outcome $x$, whatever $v$ is
Averaging the payoffs of all actions and choosing the closest

questions.question: A decision maker chooses an action $a\in A$; each action induces a probability distribution over outcomes $x$, and $v(x)$ is the payoff of outcome $x$. Action $a$ can produce only outcomes whose payoffs lie between $2$ and $9$. Which values can $\mathbb{E}[v(x)\mid a]$ take?
options: Values above $9$ if $9$ is very likely
Only values between $2$ and $9$
Only the values $2$ or $9$ themselves
Only the midpoint $5.5$ of the range

questions.question: An action yields $40$ with probability $0.1$, $20$ with probability $0.6$ and $0$ with probability $0.3$, and the payoff is $v(x)=x$. What is the expected payoff of this action?

Action Safe gives $16$ for sure; action Risky gives $36$ or $0$, each with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$. The decision maker maximises expected payoff with $v(x)=\sqrt x$. Which action is chosen, and why?
options: Safe: $\sqrt{16}=4$ exceeds $\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{36}=3$.
Risky: its expected money $18$ exceeds $16$.
Risky: $\sqrt{18}\approx4.24$ exceeds $\sqrt{16}=4$.
Neither: both give the same expected payoff.

questions.question: Under action $a_2$ the outcome has density $f(x\mid a_2)=x/450$ on $[0,30]$ (zero elsewhere), and the payoff is $v(x)=x$. What is $\mathbb{E}[v(x)\mid a_2]$?

An action is said to give outcomes $x_1,x_2,x_3$ with probabilities $p(x_1\mid a)=0.5$, $p(x_2\mid a)=0.3$ and $p(x_3\mid a)=0.3$. Can the expected payoff $\sum_k p(x_k\mid a)v(x_k)$ be used to evaluate this action?
options: Yes: each probability lies between $0$ and $1$, which suffices.
No: the probabilities sum to $1.1$, so they are not a distribution.
Yes, after dividing the expected payoff by $3$, the number of outcomes.
No: an action may not have more than two possible outcomes.

questions.question: Lottery $L_1$ has expected payoff $10$ and lottery $L_2$ has expected payoff $30$. A compound lottery runs $L_1$ with probability $0.25$ and $L_2$ with probability $0.75$. What is its expected payoff?

Under action $a$ the outcome $x$ has density $f(x\mid a)$, and the payoff is $v(x)=x^2$. To get $\mathbb{E}[v(x)\mid a]$, a student first derives the density $f_Y$ of $y=x^2$ and then computes $\int y\,f_Y(y)\,\mathrm{d}y$. Is that first step necessary?
options: Yes: an expectation of $v(x)$ is defined only via the distribution of $v(x)$.
No, but integrating $v(x)f(x\mid a)$ is valid only if $v$ is monotone.
Yes: the shortcut works for probability mass functions, not for densities.
No: one may integrate $v(x)f(x\mid a)$ directly; both routes agree.

questions.question: A decision maker chooses an action $a\in A$; each action induces a probability distribution over outcomes $x$, and $v(x)$ is the payoff of outcome $x$. The payoff $v$ is replaced by $f\circ v$. For which $f$ is the ranking of all actions guaranteed to stay the same?
options: Any strictly increasing $f$
$f(y)=\alpha y+\beta$ with any $\alpha\ne0$
$f(y)=\alpha y+\beta$ with $\alpha>0$
Any $f$ with $f(0)=0$

questions.question: A decision maker chooses an action $a\in A$; each action induces a probability distribution over outcomes $x$, and $v(x)$ is the payoff of outcome $x$. When is an action that maximises $\mathbb{E}[v(x)\mid a]$ guaranteed to exist?
options: When the set of outcomes is finite, whatever $A$ is
When the set of actions $A$ is finite
When all payoffs $v(x)$ are nonnegative
When every action has a continuous outcome distribution

questions.question: Under payoff $v$, action $a_1$ has expected payoff $12$ and action $a_2$ has expected payoff $10$. The payoff is replaced by $w(x)=50-2v(x)$. Which action maximises the expected value of $w$?
options: $a_2$, with $\mathbb{E}[w]=30$ against $26$
$a_1$, with $\mathbb{E}[w]=74$ against $70$
$a_1$, as rankings never change under affine maps
Neither: the expected values of $w$ are equal

questions.question: Action Safe pays $20$ for sure; action Risky pays $50$ with probability $p$ and $0$ otherwise. The payoff is $v(x)=x$. For which $p$ does an expected payoff maximiser strictly prefer Risky?

A decision maker chooses an action $a\in A$; each action induces a probability distribution over outcomes $x$, and $v(x)$ is the payoff of outcome $x$. If action $a$'s worst possible payoff exceeds action $b$'s best possible payoff, then $\mathbb{E}[v\mid a]>\mathbb{E}[v\mid b]$. Does the converse hold: does $\mathbb{E}[v\mid a]>\mathbb{E}[v\mid b]$ imply that $a$'s worst payoff exceeds $b$'s best?
options: Yes: a higher average forces every outcome of $a$ to beat every outcome of $b$.
Yes, whenever both actions have finitely many outcomes.
No: a larger expected payoff is compatible with overlapping payoff ranges.
No: it only implies that $a$'s best payoff exceeds $b$'s best payoff.

questions.question: Action $a_1$ makes the outcome uniform on $[0,20]$ (density $1/20$); action $a_2$ gives $10$ for sure. The payoff is $v(x)=x^2$. Which action maximises the expected payoff?
options: $a_1$, since $\mathbb{E}[x^2\mid a_1]=400/3>100$
Neither, since both have expected outcome $10$
$a_2$, since a sure outcome beats any lottery
$a_1$, since $\mathbb{E}[x^2\mid a_1]=400>100$

questions.question: Action $a_1$ gives outcome density $f(x\mid a_1)=2x$ on $[0,1]$; action $a_2$ gives the uniform density $1$ on $[0,1]$. The payoff is $v(x)=x(1-x)$. Which action does an expected payoff maximiser choose?
options: $a_1$, as its mean outcome $2/3$ exceeds $1/2$
Either: both expected payoffs equal $1/6$
$a_1$, as its density rises towards high outcomes

questions.question: A decision maker chooses an action $a\in A$; each action induces a probability distribution over outcomes $x$, and $v(x)$ is the payoff of outcome $x$. What does choosing an action determine in such a decision problem?
options: The outcome itself: every action, risky or not, fixes what happens.
The payoff function $v$: each action values the outcomes in its own way.
The set of outcomes that can occur, but not their probabilities.
The outcome's distribution; only a sure action fixes the outcome itself.
